title: Learning From a Good Place
author: Chris McColl
summary: Chris McColl revisits an earlier essay on the roles of community and ethos in the virtue education of young people. He starts from a school he once visited whose founding head wanted 'a place where it should be easy to be good', and poses a paradox: virtue education needs a plan, yet a plan seems to need an already good place to succeed. He uses the sitcom The Good Place as a loose blueprint, pairing each season with boarding-school stories. A new boarder learns he can simply sit down at a table, and a reluctant transfer student eventually accepts the friendship offered, which shows that good places stay patient and keep a hand outstretched. The Trolley Problem and a coach's story of carrying a log illustrate that choices affect others and that contribution is relative to ability. The final lesson is that schools send graduates out as an act of faith in their own communal effect, and he hopes that virtue-focused schools might form a connected network.
points: Formal virtue education cannot succeed unless the community around it is already one where it is easy to be good, so ethos is the precondition rather than an extra.
Good schools teach interdependence more than independence, asking students both to accept kindness and to become people others can rely on.
Good places are patient: they keep offering inclusion to newcomers who initially distrust it and do not judge the pace of acceptance.
The log-carrying coach and the friends who hid their higher grades show that moral contribution is relative, and that appreciating where others sit on the spectrum makes goodness easier.
Sending graduates out is an expression of faith in the school's communal effect, and schools could strengthen it by linking up as a network of virtue-based communities.
quotes: As it happens, I learned that the first head of that particular school I visited had always intended to create “a place where it should be easy to be good.

It seemed to me that you couldn’t make people improve morally and ethically without a plan for virtue education; that said, how could any virtue education plan be successful if it wasn’t the product of an already good place?
The best boarding school experiences, I think, don’t teach independence so much as interdependence – you learn to find your people and to rely on them to help you through tough times.

But good places remain patient. They continue to offer and include. We know that those new to our place need time to trust the good in themselves that others know and embrace without doubt or question.
Until that time, though, all a good place can do is keep a friendly hand outstretched and wait.
A team succeeds because everyone makes choices that contribute to that success.
They understood that accomplishment is relative: a 92 that culminates months of work can be worth more than the 98 that is easily earned.
We send them as an expression of faith in ourselves - as faith in our communal effect.
Might this create a living global network of schools and communities that truly and holistically prioritize moral behavior and human virtues?
